newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to sign "motherhood" health measure.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to sign "motherhood" health measure.

text.p: Motherhood and apple pie are said to be the only non-controversial issues in American politics, and President Bill Clinton on Thursday gets to champion the first of these.

At a White House Rose Garden ceremony, Clinton was set to sign into law a bill that requires health insurers to let new mothers stay in the hospital for 48 hours after a normal delivery and 96 hours after a Caesarean.

The measure resulted from grassroots pressure from a public fed up with health care penny-pinching that forces mothers to leave the hospital with their babies sometimes as soon as 10 hours after a normal delivery.

It is bundled into an annual money bill for the Departments of Labour and Housing and Urban Development that ordinarily would merit little attention, and certainly not the fanfare of a Rose Garden bill-signing ceremony.

Halting the practice called drive-through deliveries is a "big issue," Clinton told supporters at a rally in Pennsylvania on Wednesday. His visit coincided with a new Reuters poll that showed him leading Republican Bob Dole in the crucial state by 16 percentage points. It was yet another sign that Clinton is well positioned to triumph in the Nov. 5 election.

The legislation was approved by a Republican-controlled Congress that is increasingly putting its own interests above those of the embattled Dole. "We did not want to be branded as against 48 hours and therefore it passed," a House Republican aide said.

Later on Thursday Clinton is likely to get another lift when he visits buoyant Congressional Democrats at the U.S. Capitol. His visit comes two weeks to the day after Dole went to Capitol Hill to caution scared Republican lawmakers against becoming "faint-hearted."

Clinton's soaring political fortunes -- and Dole's backfiring effort to catch him -- are fuelling a palpable sense of smugness in the Clinton camp about the president's prospects in upcoming campaign debates.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry sarcastically described Dole on Wednesday as "this titanic juggernaut of a debater," and suggested that Clinton might have time for golf during his preparations for the first debate, which is scheduled to take place in Hartford, Connecticut on Oct. 6.
McCurry backtracked later however, saying that Dole had a good deal of experience in debates and that Clinton was taking him seriously.

Clinton and Dole aides squabbled on Wednesday over debate arrangements with Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockart saying the Dole team was putting the encounters in jeopardy. Clinton himself took a positive view.
"There'll be debates. I'm sure of it," he said when reporters asked him about the controversy.
